title: Reproductive Dysplasia and Neoplasms
subject: Reproductive System (REPR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the precancers and tumors of the cervix, endometrium, myometrium, ovary, vagina, vulva, prostate, penis, and testis. Rather than memorizing each tumor separately, learn the small number of drivers that explain most of them: high-risk HPV acting through the E6 and E7 oncoproteins, unopposed estrogen acting on the endometrium, inherited or acquired loss of tumor suppressors such as TP53, PTEN, and BRCA, and the rule that a tumor makes the products of the cell it imitates. Board cases usually give an age, a risk setting, a histologic clue, or a tumor marker and ask you to name the lesion, its precursor, or its route of spread.
prerequisites: Cell cycle control by p53 and RB, and how oncogenes and tumor suppressors cause cancer
Histology of the cervix, endometrium, ovary, testis, and prostate
Ovarian and menstrual cycle hormones: estrogen, progesterone, LH, FSH, and aromatase
Embryology of the gonads, Mullerian ducts, and testicular descent
Lymphatic and venous drainage of the pelvis and perineum

connections.to: Reproductive pathogens and sexually transmitted infections (RE-12, RE-13-K)
connections.how: HPV types 16 and 18 cause most cervical, vaginal, vulvar, and penile squamous precancers, while types 6 and 11 cause benign condylomas.
Estrogen excess, androgen excess, hCG, and thyroid hormone from tumors explain precocious puberty, virilization, gynecomastia, and hyperthyroidism.
Dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, invasion, grade, and stage are all illustrated by the cervix, endometrium, and vulva.
BRCA1, BRCA2, and Lynch syndrome link ovarian, endometrial, prostate, breast, and colon cancer within families.
Cervical cancer causes postrenal failure through ureteral obstruction, and prostate cancer produces osteoblastic bone metastases.

sections.title: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia: HPV, the transformation zone, and grading

blocks.text: The ectocervix is covered by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium and the endocervical canal by mucus-secreting columnar epithelium. At puberty and in pregnancy, estrogen everts the columnar epithelium onto the ectocervix, where the acidic vaginal environment drives squamous metaplasia. The area of metaplasia is the transformation zone. Its immature basal and reserve cells are actively dividing and easily reached through small abrasions, which is why nearly all cervical precancers and carcinomas begin there.

Human papillomavirus (HPV) infects these basal cells. Low-risk types (6 and 11) stay episomal and cause condylomas. High-risk types (16 and 18, with 31, 33, 45, and others) express two oncoproteins: E6 binds p53 and targets it for ubiquitin-mediated degradation, removing the G1 checkpoint and apoptosis, and E7 binds RB, releasing E2F and pushing the cell into S phase. Integration of high-risk viral DNA into the host genome often disrupts the viral E2 gene, which normally represses E6 and E7, so the oncoproteins are overexpressed. Inactivated RB leads to overexpression of the cell cycle inhibitor p16, so strong diffuse p16 staining is used as a tissue marker of high-risk HPV activity.

In a productive infection the virus replicates in maturing upper cells, producing koilocytes: cells with enlarged, hyperchromatic, wrinkled (raisin-like) nuclei and a clear perinuclear halo. Koilocytes therefore mark infection, not grade. Grade is set by how much of the epithelial thickness is replaced by atypical immature basal-type cells that fail to mature as they move toward the surface.

blocks.title: Grading of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia
rows: Mostly productive viral infection with koilocytes; usually regresses
True precancer; may regress, especially in young women
More than two-thirds to full thickness (includes carcinoma in situ)
Highest risk of invasion; basement membrane still intact
blocks.caption: The same LSIL and HSIL terms are used for Pap cytology, so a cytology report and a biopsy grade can be compared directly.

blocks.text: Because the basement membrane is intact in all grades, CIN cannot metastasize. Cytology (the Pap test) samples cells shed from the transformation zone, and the abnormal nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio of immature atypical cells is what the cytologist recognizes.

sections.title: Risk factors for cervical dysplasia and the natural history of CIN

blocks.text: HPV infection is very common in young sexually active people, and most infections are cleared by cell-mediated immunity within about 1 to 2 years. Dysplasia develops when a high-risk type persists. Every major risk factor works in one of two ways: it increases exposure to high-risk HPV, or it weakens the local immune response that would clear it.

blocks.title: Risk factors for cervical dysplasia and how they act
rows: Continued E6 and E7 expression; HPV 16 and 18 together cause about 70% of cervical cancers, and HPV 18 is relatively more common in adenocarcinoma
Exposure while the transformation zone is large and metaplasia is most active
Many sexual partners, or a partner with many partners
Tobacco carcinogens concentrate in cervical mucus, and smoking reduces local immune cells such as Langerhans cells
Poor cell-mediated clearance; persistent, multifocal, faster-progressing lesions
Long-term oral contraceptive use and high parity (secondary factors)
Associated with higher risk among HPV-positive women; mechanism not fully settled
blocks.caption: HPV is necessary but not sufficient. The other factors determine whether infection persists and progresses.

blocks.text: Most CIN 1 regresses: in about 60% the lesion disappears, about 30% persist, and only about 10% progress to HSIL. CIN 1 is largely a sign of a productive infection that the immune system usually removes. HSIL regresses less often (roughly a third) and progresses to invasive carcinoma in a minority over years. Progression from infection to invasive cancer usually takes a decade or more, which is why periodic screening works: there is a long window in which an intraepithelial lesion can be found.

In HIV infection, lesions are more often high grade, multifocal, and extend to the vagina, vulva, and anus, because the same virus infects all of these squamous surfaces and is not cleared. Invasive cervical carcinoma is an AIDS-defining illness.

blocks.predict: A 23-year-old with CIN 1 on biopsy and a 45-year-old with HIV and CIN 1 on biopsy are followed for two years. Which lesion is more likely to persist or progress?
blocks.explain: The woman with HIV. Clearance of HPV depends on cell-mediated immunity, so poor T cell function lets high-risk HPV persist and keeps E6 and E7 active, whereas the immunocompetent young woman will usually clear the infection and the lesion will regress.

sections.title: Invasive cervical carcinoma and ureteral obstruction

blocks.text: Invasive carcinoma begins when atypical cells break through the basement membrane into the cervical stroma. About 75 to 80% are squamous cell carcinomas arising from HSIL in the transformation zone. About 15 to 20% are adenocarcinomas arising from adenocarcinoma in situ of the endocervical glands; their share has grown because glandular precursors high in the canal are sampled less reliably by cytology. Adenosquamous and neuroendocrine (small cell) carcinomas are uncommon. Both main types are driven by high-risk HPV.

Early invasive cancer is often silent. As the tumor grows into a friable exophytic or ulcerated mass, contact during intercourse makes it bleed, so postcoital bleeding is the classic symptom, along with irregular or postmenopausal bleeding and a watery or foul discharge from necrotic tumor.

blocks.title: High-risk HPV to invasive cervical carcinoma and renal failure
steps: High-risk HPV infects basal cells of the transformation zone
Viral DNA integrates; E6 and E7 are overexpressed
E6 degrades p53; E7 inactivates RB
Atypical immature cells expand from CIN 1 to CIN 3
Cells breach the basement membrane and invade stroma
Lateral spread into the parametrium encases the ureters
Bilateral hydronephrosis causes postrenal failure and uremia
blocks.caption: Lateral spread, not distant metastasis, is a leading cause of death in advanced cervical cancer.

blocks.text: The anatomy explains the complication. The parametrium is the connective tissue beside the cervix within the base of the broad ligament (the cardinal ligament region). Each ureter runs through it about 1.5 to 2 cm lateral to the cervix, passing beneath the uterine artery. Tumor extending laterally compresses and encases the ureters. Obstruction raises pressure above the block, dilating the ureter and renal pelvis (hydroureter and hydronephrosis); sustained back pressure lowers the glomerular filtration rate and causes pressure atrophy of the renal parenchyma. When both ureters are blocked, blood urea nitrogen and creatinine rise as postrenal azotemia progresses to uremia, a leading cause of death in advanced disease. Hydronephrosis from tumor is a criterion for advanced (stage III) disease.

Other routes follow the same local logic: anterior growth into the bladder and posterior growth into the rectum cause hematuria, fistulas, and rectal bleeding; lymphatic spread goes to paracervical, obturator, and internal and external iliac nodes, then common iliac and para-aortic nodes. Pelvic sidewall involvement causes back or sciatic pain and leg edema from lymphatic and venous obstruction.

sections.title: Endometrial hyperplasia: unopposed estrogen and PTEN loss

blocks.text: Estrogen, acting through estrogen receptor alpha, drives proliferation of endometrial glands and stroma in the first half of the cycle. After ovulation, progesterone from the corpus luteum opposes this: it stops proliferation, converts the glands to secretory endometrium, reduces estrogen receptor levels, and increases the enzyme that converts estradiol to the weaker estrone. When the corpus luteum fails, progesterone withdrawal causes orderly shedding. Endometrial hyperplasia is an increase in the ratio of glands to stroma caused by estrogen stimulation that is not opposed by progesterone.

blocks.title: Sources of unopposed estrogen
rows: Aromatase in adipose stroma converts adrenal androstenedione to estrone; insulin resistance lowers sex hormone binding globulin, raising free estrogen
No ovulation means no corpus luteum and no progesterone, while follicles still make estrogen; PCOS adds high androgen for peripheral aromatization
Exogenous estrogen given without a progestin to a woman with a uterus
Antagonist at breast estrogen receptors but partial agonist at endometrial receptors
blocks.caption: Each cause raises estrogen action or removes the progesterone that normally limits it.

blocks.title: Unopposed estrogen to endometrioid carcinoma
steps: Estrogen acts without progesterone
Glands proliferate continuously without secretory change or shedding
Dividing cells accumulate mutations, most often PTEN loss
PI3K/AKT signaling increases growth and survival
Hyperplasia without atypia
Atypical hyperplasia (endometrioid intraepithelial neoplasia)
Endometrioid adenocarcinoma
blocks.caption: A continuum from a reversible hormonal response to a clonal precancer to carcinoma.

blocks.text: PTEN is a lipid phosphatase that removes a phosphate from PIP3, opposing PI3K. When PTEN is lost, PIP3 accumulates and AKT is activated, promoting proliferation and inhibiting apoptosis. PTEN-null glands are already found in many hyperplasias, which shows that hyperplasia is not purely hormonal but is often an early clonal step.

Current classification divides hyperplasia into two groups. Hyperplasia without atypia is a diffuse, polyclonal response to estrogen with crowded but cytologically normal glands; it carries a low risk of carcinoma (about 1 to 3%) and often regresses when the estrogen excess is removed. Atypical hyperplasia, also called endometrioid intraepithelial neoplasia, is clonal, with crowded back-to-back glands and nuclear atypia; a large fraction of women with it already have, or will develop, endometrioid carcinoma. Hyperplasia presents with heavy, prolonged, or irregular bleeding, or with postmenopausal bleeding. Bleeding occurs because the thick proliferative lining outgrows its blood supply and breaks down irregularly instead of shedding in an organized way.

sections.title: Endometrioid versus serous endometrial carcinoma

blocks.text: Endometrial carcinoma is the most common invasive gynecologic cancer in the United States. It follows two main pathways that differ in cause, precursor, genetics, and behavior, and the distinction is one of the most tested ideas in gynecologic pathology.

blocks.title: Two pathways of endometrial carcinoma
rows: Perimenopausal or early postmenopausal, about 55 to 65
Estrogen excess: obesity, diabetes, anovulation, nulliparity
PTEN (most common), PIK3CA, KRAS, ARID1A; mismatch repair defects
Glands resembling normal endometrium, often well differentiated
Papillae with marked nuclear atypia; psammoma bodies possible
Usually confined to uterus at diagnosis; good prognosis
Spreads early through tubes and peritoneum even when small; poor prognosis
blocks.caption: Both types present with postmenopausal or abnormal bleeding, so the bleeding does not tell them apart; the setting and histology do.

blocks.text: Mismatch repair defects matter in endometrioid carcinoma. Mismatch repair proteins (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) correct base mispairs made during DNA replication. When they fail, errors accumulate in short repeated sequences (microsatellite instability) and in growth genes. In sporadic tumors the usual cause is silencing of MLH1 by promoter hypermethylation. In Lynch syndrome, a germline mutation in one mismatch repair gene is inherited, and loss of the second allele in the endometrium starts the tumor. Women with Lynch syndrome have a lifetime endometrial cancer risk that equals or exceeds their colon cancer risk, so endometrial carcinoma can be the sentinel cancer in a family.

Serous carcinoma explains a classic exam trap: a thin, atrophic endometrium does not protect an older woman. Because TP53-mutant cells grow without needing estrogen, the tumor can arise on an atrophic surface, exfoliate through the tubes, and seed the peritoneum, behaving much like high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma, with which it shares TP53 mutation and papillary architecture.

Postmenopausal bleeding is never normal, because a postmenopausal endometrium should be thin and inactive. It is explained by atrophy in most women, but endometrial carcinoma is the diagnosis that must be excluded. Endometrial carcinoma spreads by direct myometrial invasion, then to the cervix, pelvic and para-aortic nodes, and in serous type to the peritoneum and omentum.

sections.title: Endometrial and endocervical polyps

blocks.text: A polyp is a localized, benign overgrowth that projects from a mucosal surface. Endometrial and endocervical polyps both contain glands and stroma, but they differ in origin and setting.

Endometrial polyps are sessile or pedunculated masses, usually 0.5 to 3 cm, made of endometrial glands, dense fibrous stroma, and characteristic thick-walled blood vessels. The stromal cells are clonal and often carry chromosomal rearrangements, so the stroma is the true neoplastic component and the glands are drawn in. Polyps respond to estrogen and are more common around and after menopause, with obesity, and with tamoxifen, whose partial agonist action stimulates the endometrium. Their glands often do not respond to the cycle normally and may be hyperplastic.

Endocervical polyps are the most common cervical growths. They are smooth, soft, often red masses that protrude through the external os, composed of loose fibromyxomatous stroma covered by mucus-secreting endocervical columnar epithelium, often with chronic inflammation. They are thought to arise from inflammatory hyperplasia of the endocervix and have essentially no malignant potential.

blocks.title: Endometrial and endocervical polyps compared
rows: Endocervical canal, may protrude through the os
Endometrial glands, fibrous stroma, thick-walled vessels
Endocervical mucinous glands, loose inflamed stroma
Low; a small risk of carcinoma within a polyp, higher after menopause
blocks.caption: Both are benign, but a polyp found with postmenopausal bleeding still requires tissue diagnosis.

blocks.text: The bleeding mechanism is the same in both. The surface of a polyp is fragile; its tip may become congested as the stalk twists or is compressed, and the surface erodes or ulcerates. Contact (intercourse or examination) or ischemic breakdown then causes bleeding that is unrelated to the timing of menstruation, which is why polyps classically cause intermenstrual or postcoital spotting. An endometrial polyp can also enlarge the bleeding surface of the cavity and add to menstrual flow.

sections.title: Leiomyoma (fibroid)

blocks.text: A leiomyoma is a benign tumor of myometrial smooth muscle and the most common benign tumor in women; by age 50 most women have at least one, though many cause no symptoms. Each fibroid is monoclonal, arising from a single smooth muscle cell. The most common driver is a mutation in MED12, a subunit of the transcriptional Mediator complex; others carry HMGA2 rearrangements, and inherited fumarate hydratase mutations cause multiple leiomyomas with renal cell carcinoma.

Growth depends on ovarian hormones. Estrogen increases progesterone receptors and growth factor signaling, and progesterone itself promotes fibroid cell proliferation and extracellular matrix production. This explains the natural history: fibroids appear after menarche, can enlarge in pregnancy, and shrink after menopause when ovarian hormone production falls. They are diagnosed at a younger age, are larger and more numerous, and cause more symptoms in Black women, in whom the incidence is about two to three times higher.

Grossly, leiomyomas are firm, sharply circumscribed, gray-white masses that bulge from the cut surface with a whorled pattern from interlacing smooth muscle bundles. They lack a true capsule but are surrounded by compressed myometrium (a pseudocapsule), so they shell out easily. Microscopically, uniform spindle cells with cigar-shaped nuclei form fascicles with few mitoses and no necrosis. Large fibroids outgrow their blood supply and degenerate: hyaline or cystic change, red (hemorrhagic) degeneration in pregnancy with acute pain, and calcification after menopause.

blocks.title: Fibroid location predicts symptoms
rows: Heavy menstrual bleeding, iron deficiency anemia, infertility, miscarriage
Distorts and enlarges the cavity, increasing the bleeding endometrial surface and impairing implantation
Heavy bleeding, enlarged irregular uterus, pelvic pressure
Enlarges the uterus and interferes with myometrial contraction that limits bleeding
Pressure on bladder (frequency) or rectum (constipation), torsion pain
Mass effect on neighboring organs; a pedunculated fibroid can twist on its stalk
blocks.caption: Most women have fibroids in more than one location.

blocks.text: Heavy menstrual bleeding is the most important symptom because chronic blood loss depletes iron stores, producing microcytic, hypochromic anemia with low ferritin. In pregnancy, fibroids are linked to miscarriage, malpresentation, obstructed labor, and postpartum hemorrhage, the last because they prevent the uterus from contracting uniformly after delivery.

sections.title: Leiomyosarcoma versus leiomyoma

blocks.text: Leiomyosarcoma is a rare malignant smooth muscle tumor of the uterus, typically in women in their 40s to 60s, often postmenopausal. It arises de novo from myometrium or its precursor cells. Leiomyomas do not transform into leiomyosarcomas: the two tumors have different genetic profiles (leiomyosarcomas have complex karyotypes with frequent TP53 and RB pathway disruption, whereas leiomyomas have simple changes such as MED12 mutation). A woman with many fibroids is therefore not at increased risk of sarcoma because of those fibroids.

blocks.title: Leiomyoma and leiomyosarcoma compared
rows: Large, soft, fleshy, with hemorrhage and necrosis; infiltrative borders
Many (often 10 or more per 10 high-power fields)
Hematogenous, most often to the lungs; frequent recurrence
blocks.caption: The diagnosis rests on combining atypia, mitotic rate, and tumor cell necrosis; usually at least two of the three are required.

blocks.text: Necrosis must be read carefully. A degenerating fibroid can show infarct-type necrosis with a rim of granulation tissue, because a benign tumor outgrew its supply. Coagulative tumor cell necrosis in a sarcoma shows an abrupt transition from viable atypical cells to dead cells, because a fast-growing malignant clone outruns its vessels throughout the tumor.

Clinically, leiomyosarcoma cannot be reliably separated from a fibroid before surgery. A uterine mass that grows rapidly after menopause, when fibroids should shrink, is the classic warning sign, because a hormone-dependent benign tumor should not enlarge once estrogen and progesterone fall. Spread is hematogenous, like most sarcomas, rather than lymphatic, which explains early lung metastases. Prognosis is poor, with roughly 40% five-year survival overall and much better outcomes when the tumor is confined to the uterus.

sections.title: Prostate adenocarcinoma: risk, zonal origin, grading, and PSA

blocks.text: Prostatic adenocarcinoma is the most common noncutaneous cancer in men and a leading cause of cancer death in men. Incidence rises steeply with age, and many older men have small, clinically silent tumors at autopsy. Incidence and mortality are highest in Black men. Risk is increased by a family history in first-degree relatives and by germline mutations, most importantly BRCA2, which is associated with earlier and more aggressive disease. The tumor depends on androgen signaling: testosterone is converted by 5-alpha-reductase to dihydrotestosterone, which drives growth through the androgen receptor. A common early genetic event is fusion of the androgen-regulated TMPRSS2 promoter to an ETS family transcription factor gene such as ERG, so androgen directly switches on an oncogene.

About 70 to 80% of carcinomas arise in the peripheral zone, the posterior and lateral part of the gland that lies against the rectum. That location explains two findings: the tumor can be felt as a hard, irregular nodule on digital rectal examination, and it rarely causes early urinary obstruction because it is away from the urethra. Benign prostatic hyperplasia, by contrast, arises in the periurethral transition zone and obstructs early. The precursor is high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia.

Microscopically, carcinoma forms small, crowded glands lined by a single layer of cells with enlarged nuclei and prominent nucleoli. The key diagnostic point is the absence of the basal cell layer that surrounds benign glands; stains for basal cells (p63, high molecular weight keratin) are negative, and the tumor cells express AMACR. Perineural invasion is common.

Gleason grading is based on gland architecture, not nuclear detail. Each pattern is graded from 1 (well formed, uniform glands) to 5 (no glands, sheets or single cells). The score adds the most common (primary) and second most common pattern, so 3 + 4 = 7. In practice scores now range from 6 to 10, and they are grouped into Grade Groups 1 (score 6) to 5 (score 9 or 10). Higher scores predict spread and death.

blocks.title: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) and what raises it
rows: A serine protease (a kallikrein) made by normal and malignant prostatic epithelium that liquefies semen
Disrupted gland architecture and basement membrane let it leak into the circulation; cancer releases more per gram of tissue
About 4 ng/mL, with age-adjusted ranges; no value fully separates cancer from benign disease
Benign causes of a raised PSA
Benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostatitis, infarction, urinary retention, instrumentation, and recent ejaculation
5-alpha-reductase inhibition shrinks the gland and lowers PSA by about half
Cancer releases relatively more bound PSA, so a low free PSA fraction favors cancer
blocks.caption: PSA is organ-specific, not cancer-specific.

sections.title: Osteoblastic bone metastases of prostate carcinoma

blocks.text: Bone is the most common site of distant spread from prostate cancer, and the lumbar spine and pelvis are the bones most often involved, followed by the proximal femur and ribs. Anatomy explains the pattern. The prostatic venous plexus drains into the internal iliac veins, but it also connects freely with the vertebral venous plexus (Batson plexus), a network of valveless veins around the spinal column. When intra-abdominal pressure rises with coughing or straining, blood in the pelvic veins can flow backward into this plexus, carrying tumor cells straight to the lumbar vertebrae and pelvis without passing through the lungs.

blocks.title: Prostate carcinoma to osteoblastic bone metastases
steps: Peripheral zone carcinoma invades the prostatic venous plexus
Valveless vertebral veins carry cells to the lumbar spine and pelvis
Tumor cells settle in red marrow
Tumor secretes factors such as endothelin-1 and BMPs
Osteoblasts lay down new, disorganized woven bone
Sclerotic lesions, bone pain, raised alkaline phosphatase
blocks.caption: Prostate cancer is the classic cause of osteoblastic (sclerotic) metastases in men.

blocks.text: Most carcinomas that metastasize to bone, such as lung, kidney, and thyroid, are osteolytic: they stimulate osteoclasts, often through RANKL and PTHrP, and destroy bone. Prostate cancer is the classic exception. Its cells secrete osteoblast-stimulating factors, including endothelin-1 and bone morphogenetic proteins, so new bone is laid down around the tumor. The new bone is woven and poorly organized, so it is dense on imaging but mechanically weak. Even sclerotic lesions have an underlying increase in resorption, which is why fractures still occur. Breast cancer can produce lytic, blastic, or mixed lesions.

Each laboratory and clinical finding follows from osteoblast activity. Osteoblasts express alkaline phosphatase, so serum alkaline phosphatase (bone isoenzyme) rises with active bone formation. Radionuclide bone scans show intense uptake because the tracer binds to sites of new mineralization, and plain films show dense vertebrae. Serum calcium is usually normal and can even fall, because calcium is taken up into the new bone, in contrast to the hypercalcemia typical of lytic metastases. Pain arises from periosteal stretch and marrow infiltration. Collapse of an involved vertebra or epidural tumor can compress the spinal cord or cauda equina, causing back pain, leg weakness, and bladder or bowel dysfunction.

blocks.title: Telling blastic from lytic metastases
blocks.text: A 72-year-old man has low back pain. Imaging shows several dense lumbar vertebrae, alkaline phosphatase is high, and calcium is 8.9 mg/dL (reference about 8.5 to 10.2). Work through it: dense bone means osteoblasts are being driven, not osteoclasts. Raised alkaline phosphatase confirms osteoblast activity. Normal calcium fits, because new bone takes calcium in rather than releasing it. Spine plus pelvis in an older man points to Batson plexus spread from the prostate. A lytic pattern with hypercalcemia would instead suggest myeloma, lung, kidney, or breast primary.

sections.title: Classification of ovarian tumors by cell of origin

blocks.text: The ovary contains three tissues that can give rise to tumors, and each tumor resembles the tissue it comes from. Surface epithelial tumors arise from Mullerian-type epithelium (the ovarian surface, inclusion cysts, endometriosis, or the fallopian tube). Germ cell tumors arise from oocytes and copy embryonic or extraembryonic tissues. Sex cord-stromal tumors arise from the cells of the follicle and ovarian stroma that make hormones. Knowing the origin predicts age, behavior, and what the tumor secretes.

blocks.title: Ovarian tumors by origin
rows: About two-thirds of all, about 90% of malignant
Serous, mucinous, endometrioid, clear cell, Brenner
Teratoma (mature, immature, monodermal), dysgerminoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma, embryonal carcinoma
AFP, hCG, LDH by type; thyroid hormone in struma ovarii
Granulosa cell, Sertoli-Leydig cell, fibroma, thecoma
blocks.caption: Most ovarian tumors are benign; the malignant ones are mostly epithelial.

blocks.text: Surface epithelial tumors are further graded as benign (cystadenoma), borderline (low malignant potential, with atypia but no destructive stromal invasion), or malignant (carcinoma). The subtypes differ in their lining. Serous tumors have tubal-type ciliated or papillary epithelium; mucinous tumors form large multiloculated cysts lined by mucin-secreting cells resembling endocervix or intestine, often unilateral and sometimes very large; endometrioid and clear cell carcinomas often arise from endometriosis and share mutations such as ARID1A; Brenner tumors contain nests of urothelium-like cells with grooved coffee-bean nuclei in a fibrous stroma and are usually benign.

Epithelial cancer risk rises with nulliparity, family history, BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation, Lynch syndrome, and endometriosis (for endometrioid and clear cell types), and falls with oral contraceptive use, multiparity, breastfeeding, and tubal ligation. The protective factors share a theme: fewer ovulations, or less exposure of tube and ovary to repeated injury and repair, means fewer chances for mutation in Mullerian epithelium.

sections.title: High-grade serous carcinoma: genetics, tubal origin, and spread

blocks.text: High-grade serous carcinoma is the most common and most lethal ovarian cancer. TP53 is mutated in nearly every case, and germline or somatic BRCA1 or BRCA2 loss is present in a substantial fraction. BRCA1 and BRCA2 are needed for homologous recombination, the error-free repair of double-strand DNA breaks. Without them, cells repair breaks by error-prone pathways and accumulate chromosomal damage, and loss of p53 lets these damaged cells survive instead of undergoing apoptosis. The result is a genetically unstable, high-grade tumor. Women with a BRCA1 mutation have a lifetime ovarian cancer risk of about 40%, and with BRCA2 about 10 to 20%.

Many of these cancers begin in the fallopian tube, not the ovary. Serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma, a TP53-mutant intraepithelial lesion of the fimbria, is found in a large share of tubes removed from BRCA carriers and of women with pelvic serous carcinoma. The fimbria lies on the ovary, so cells shed from the tube implant on the ovarian surface and peritoneum. By contrast, low-grade serous carcinoma is a different disease that arises from serous borderline tumors, carries KRAS or BRAF mutations, and grows slowly.

Histologically the tumor forms papillae and solid sheets with marked nuclear atypia. Psammoma bodies, laminated calcifications formed when single tumor cells or papillary tips die and calcify, are a classic clue to serous papillary tumors, and they also appear in papillary thyroid carcinoma and meningioma.

blocks.title: How serous carcinoma spreads through the peritoneum
steps: Carcinoma arises in the tubal fimbria or ovarian surface
Tumor cells exfoliate into peritoneal fluid
Fluid circulation carries cells to omentum, diaphragm, and bowel
Implants grow into an omental cake and peritoneal nodules
Blocked diaphragmatic lymphatics and leaky vessels cause ascites
Abdominal distension, bloating, early satiety, bowel obstruction
blocks.caption: Spread is mainly transcoelomic, which is why most patients have peritoneal disease at diagnosis.

blocks.text: Because the peritoneal cavity offers no barrier, symptoms are late and vague: bloating, abdominal fullness, early satiety, and urinary frequency. Most women are diagnosed with disease beyond the pelvis. CA-125 (MUC16) is a glycoprotein expressed by coelomic and Mullerian epithelium; it is raised (above about 35 U/mL) in most women with advanced serous carcinoma but in only about half with early disease, and it also rises in endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease, pregnancy, menstruation, cirrhosis with ascites, and any peritoneal irritation. It is therefore a marker for following known disease, not a screening test.

blocks.predict: A 46-year-old woman with a BRCA1 mutation has bloating, ascites, and a CA-125 of 600 U/mL, but both ovaries are only slightly enlarged at surgery while the omentum is full of tumor. How can a small ovary produce such widespread disease?
blocks.explain: High-grade serous carcinoma often begins in the tubal fimbria and spreads by exfoliation into peritoneal fluid, so it seeds the omentum and peritoneum early without forming a large ovarian mass. BRCA1 loss with TP53 mutation makes the tumor genetically unstable and aggressive from the start.
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraph on tubal origin and the peritoneal spread flow.

sections.title: Ovarian germ cell tumors: teratoma, struma ovarii, dysgerminoma, yolk sac tumor

blocks.text: Germ cell tumors arise from oocytes and mimic the tissues an early embryo can make. Tissues of the embryo proper form teratoma; undifferentiated germ cells form dysgerminoma; extraembryonic yolk sac forms yolk sac tumor, and trophoblast forms choriocarcinoma. Each tumor type therefore secretes the product of the tissue it copies, and that is the basis of the tumor markers.

Mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst) is the most common ovarian germ cell tumor and one of the most common ovarian tumors of young women. It is benign. It arises from a germ cell after the first meiotic division, so it is usually 46,XX. The cyst is lined by skin with hair follicles and sebaceous glands and is filled with sebum and hair; teeth, cartilage, bone, respiratory epithelium, and neural tissue are common, usually concentrated in a nodule on the wall. About 10 to 15% are bilateral. Complications follow from its weight and contents: torsion with sudden severe pain, rupture with chemical peritonitis from sebum, rare malignant transformation (usually squamous cell carcinoma, in older women), and anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis when the neural tissue provokes antibodies that cross-react with brain receptors. Immature teratoma, which contains primitive embryonic tissue (especially immature neuroepithelium), is malignant.

Struma ovarii is a monodermal teratoma composed mainly or entirely of mature thyroid tissue. That tissue makes thyroid hormone independently of TSH, so a minority of patients become hyperthyroid with low TSH and a normal-sized thyroid.

blocks.title: Ovarian germ cell tumors and their markers
rows: Skin, hair, sebum, teeth, neural tissue
Adolescents and young women; gonadal dysgenesis
Sheets of large clear cells, fibrous septa with lymphocytes
blocks.caption: Dysgerminoma is the ovarian counterpart of testicular seminoma.

blocks.text: Dysgerminoma is the most common malignant ovarian germ cell tumor. Its uniform clear cells are rich in glycogen, and lymphocytes infiltrate the fibrous septa, exactly as in seminoma. It is linked to gonadal dysgenesis with Y chromosome material, and LDH is the usual serum marker. Yolk sac tumor is identified by Schiller-Duval bodies, glomerulus-like structures in which a central blood vessel is wrapped by tumor cells within a space also lined by tumor cells. Like fetal yolk sac, it secretes alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), visible as hyaline globules.

sections.title: Hormonally active ovarian stromal tumors and Meigs syndrome

blocks.text: Sex cord-stromal tumors copy the hormone-producing cells of the gonad, so their clinical effects are predicted by the hormone they make and by the age of the patient. In the normal follicle, theca cells make androgen under LH, and granulosa cells convert it to estradiol with aromatase under FSH. Leydig cells make testosterone, and Sertoli cells support germ cells.

Granulosa cell tumors produce estrogen. The adult type, which carries a FOXL2 mutation in nearly all cases, usually occurs in peri- and postmenopausal women; a juvenile type occurs in children. Microscopically the cells have grooved coffee-bean nuclei and may form Call-Exner bodies, small follicle-like spaces containing eosinophilic material. They secrete inhibin, a useful marker. They are low-grade malignancies that can recur many years later.

blocks.title: Effects of a granulosa cell tumor depend on age
rows: Precocious pseudopuberty: breast development, vaginal bleeding, advanced bone age
Estrogen comes from the tumor, so it is GnRH-independent and LH and FSH are suppressed
Excess estrogen disrupts the cycle and stimulates the endometrium
Endometrial hyperplasia, endometrial carcinoma, breast tenderness, postmenopausal bleeding
Unopposed estrogen acts on an endometrium with no progesterone
blocks.caption: Thecomas, made of lipid-laden theca-like cells in postmenopausal women, can also produce estrogen with the same endometrial effects.

blocks.text: Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors occur mainly in young women and secrete androgens. The effects come in sequence: first defeminization (amenorrhea, breast atrophy, loss of female fat distribution) as androgen suppresses the cycle, then virilization (hirsutism, clitoromegaly, deepening voice, temporal balding). Some are associated with DICER1 mutations.

Fibroma is a benign, hormonally inactive tumor of ovarian stromal fibroblasts that forms a hard, white, solid mass. Meigs syndrome is the combination of an ovarian fibroma (or another benign solid ovarian tumor), ascites, and a pleural effusion, usually right-sided. The fluid is thought to leak from the tumor surface into the peritoneum and then pass to the pleural space through diaphragmatic lymphatics and small diaphragmatic defects, which are more common on the right. The ascites and effusion resolve after the tumor is removed. Meigs syndrome matters because it mimics disseminated ovarian cancer: a pelvic mass with ascites and a pleural effusion that turns out to be benign.

blocks.title: Matching a hormone to a tumor
blocks.text: A 7-year-old girl has breast development, vaginal bleeding, and a right adnexal mass; LH and FSH are low. Reason it through: puberty-like changes with low gonadotropins mean the estrogen is not coming from activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis (that would be central precocious puberty with high LH and FSH). The source must be autonomous, and an adnexal mass that makes estrogen is a granulosa cell tumor, most likely the juvenile type. If the same mass made androgen, she would show virilization instead, pointing to a Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor.

sections.title: Krukenberg tumor

blocks.text: A Krukenberg tumor is a metastatic carcinoma to the ovaries composed of mucin-producing signet ring cells in a reactive, cellular ovarian stroma. It is usually bilateral. The most common primary site is the stomach, specifically diffuse-type gastric carcinoma; other sources include the colon, appendix, and breast (lobular carcinoma). A Krukenberg tumor is sometimes found before the primary tumor is known.

Signet ring cells form because the tumor cells fill with intracellular mucin, which pushes the nucleus to the edge. In diffuse gastric carcinoma, loss of E-cadherin (CDH1) prevents cells from sticking to one another, so they infiltrate as single cells rather than forming glands, a pattern that persists in the ovarian metastasis. Mucin stains such as PAS and mucicarmine highlight the vacuoles. The ovaries are enlarged and solid, often keeping their outline, and the stroma around the tumor cells can become luteinized and occasionally produce androgen or estrogen.

The route of spread is not fully settled; lymphatic, hematogenous, and transcoelomic routes have all been proposed. The bilateral, often symmetric involvement and frequent peritoneal disease support spread through lymphatics and peritoneal fluid.

blocks.title: Bilateral mucinous ovarian masses: metastatic or primary?
rows: Often a very large multiloculated cyst
Single signet ring cells infiltrating stroma
Cysts and glands lined by mucinous epithelium
Stomach most often; colon, appendix, breast
blocks.caption: Bilateral mucinous tumors should prompt a search for a gastrointestinal primary.

blocks.text: The general lesson extends beyond Krukenberg tumor: bilateral solid ovarian masses in a woman with gastrointestinal symptoms, weight loss, or a known carcinoma should be considered metastatic until shown otherwise. Mucinous tumors of the appendix that spread through the peritoneum cause pseudomyxoma peritonei, a different pattern of gelatinous ascites.

sections.title: Squamous cell carcinoma of the penis and its in situ forms

blocks.text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the penis is uncommon in the United States and more common where circumcision is rare. It usually affects men over 50 and arises on the glans or inner surface of the foreskin. Two pathways mirror those of the vulva. In the HPV-related pathway, high-risk HPV, most often type 16, drives the tumor through E6 and E7 exactly as in the cervix; these tumors tend to be basaloid or warty. In the HPV-independent pathway, chronic inflammation and lichen sclerosus produce keratinizing carcinomas.

blocks.title: Risk factors for penile squamous cell carcinoma
rows: E6 degrades p53 and E7 inactivates RB in infected keratinocytes
The foreskin retains smegma and moisture and harbors HPV; neonatal circumcision is protective
Trapped smegma, poor hygiene, and chronic balanoposthitis cause ongoing inflammation and epithelial injury
Tobacco carcinogens and local immune suppression
Chronic inflammatory scarring that favors HPV-independent carcinoma
blocks.caption: Like the cervix, HPV is one road to cancer; chronic inflammation is the other.

blocks.text: Three lesions represent squamous carcinoma in situ (penile intraepithelial neoplasia), and boards distinguish them by appearance and patient. All show full-thickness atypia of the epidermis with an intact basement membrane, and all are associated with HPV, mainly type 16.

blocks.title: Carcinoma in situ of the penis
rows: Solitary, sharply marked gray-white or scaly plaque
Can progress to invasive carcinoma in a minority
Older men; glans and inner foreskin
Single or multiple bright red, velvety plaques
Multiple small reddish-brown papules, often mistaken for warts
Rarely if ever progresses; often regresses
blocks.caption: Bowenoid papulosis looks like carcinoma in situ under the microscope but behaves benignly, so age and lesion number matter.

blocks.text: Invasive carcinoma presents as a painless ulcer or an exophytic, warty mass, often hidden under a phimotic foreskin and so found late. It spreads first by lymphatics to the superficial and then deep inguinal nodes, following the drainage of penile skin, and only later to pelvic nodes and distant sites. Enlarged inguinal nodes may be metastatic or reactive to infection of the ulcerated tumor.

sections.title: Testicular tumors: classification, origin, and presentation

blocks.text: Testicular tumors are the most common solid cancers in men aged about 15 to 35. About 95% are germ cell tumors; the rest are mainly sex cord-stromal tumors (Leydig and Sertoli cell tumors) and, in older men, lymphoma.

Most adult germ cell tumors develop from germ cell neoplasia in situ (GCNIS), malignant germ cells lying within seminiferous tubules along the basement membrane. GCNIS is thought to arise from fetal gonocytes that failed to mature, which is why the risk is set early in life and linked to abnormal testicular development. Nearly all invasive germ cell tumors carry extra copies of the short arm of chromosome 12, most often as isochromosome 12p, a chromosome made of two 12p arms. Genes on 12p that maintain pluripotency are thought to drive the tumor. GCNIS-derived tumors are divided into seminoma and nonseminomatous germ cell tumors (embryonal carcinoma, postpubertal yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma, teratoma, and mixed tumors). Prepubertal teratoma and yolk sac tumor, and spermatocytic tumor of older men, do not arise from GCNIS.

blocks.title: Risk factors for testicular germ cell tumors
rows: Risk is several-fold higher in the undescended testis and modestly higher in the descended one, pointing to an underlying developmental defect
Abnormal gonads retain immature germ cells
Increased germ cell tumor risk, especially mediastinal germ cell tumors
Risk in the opposite testis is increased
Brothers and sons of affected men have higher risk
blocks.caption: Infertility and other signs of testicular dysgenesis also travel with these tumors.

blocks.text: The classic presentation is a painless, firm testicular mass or heaviness in a young man. Transillumination separates solid from fluid: light passes through a fluid-filled hydrocele or spermatocele, but a solid tumor blocks it. Pain or a sudden enlargement can occur with hemorrhage into the tumor.

Lymphatic spread follows embryology. The testis develops on the posterior abdominal wall and descends, carrying its vessels and lymphatics with it, so testicular lymph drains to the para-aortic (retroperitoneal) nodes near the renal veins, not to the inguinal nodes. Scrotal skin drains to the superficial inguinal nodes. Seminoma tends to spread by lymphatics; nonseminomatous tumors, especially choriocarcinoma, spread early through blood to the lungs, liver, and brain.

sections.title: Seminoma and nonseminomatous germ cell tumors

blocks.text: Seminoma is the most common pure testicular germ cell tumor, with a peak in the 30s, slightly later than nonseminomatous tumors. It forms a homogeneous, gray-white, lobulated mass with little hemorrhage or necrosis. Microscopically it consists of sheets of uniform large cells with clear, glycogen-rich cytoplasm, central nuclei with prominent nucleoli, and fibrous septa infiltrated by lymphocytes, sometimes with granulomas. The cells express placental alkaline phosphatase (PLAP), KIT (CD117), and OCT3/4. Seminoma is very sensitive to radiation and chemotherapy, and its prognosis is excellent because it grows slowly and spreads in an orderly way through lymphatics.

Tumor markers follow the tissue each component imitates. Yolk sac elements make AFP, as fetal yolk sac does, and syncytiotrophoblast makes hCG, as placenta does. Pure seminoma never raises AFP. A minority of seminomas contain scattered syncytiotrophoblastic giant cells and raise hCG modestly. An elevated AFP in a tumor called seminoma therefore means a nonseminomatous component is present. Many germ cell tumors are mixed, and the most aggressive component determines behavior.

blocks.title: Testicular germ cell tumors compared
rows: Homogeneous mass; sheets of clear cells, lymphocytes in septa
PLAP; hCG sometimes mildly raised; AFP normal
Hemorrhagic, necrotic mass; primitive glands and sheets
CD30 positive; hCG or AFP when mixed
Boys under about 3 (pure form); common component of adult mixed tumors
Malignant; most common testicular tumor in young children
Small hemorrhagic tumor; cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast
Early blood-borne spread to lungs and brain
Tissues from two or more germ layers
In postpubertal men, malignant potential regardless of maturity
blocks.caption: Seminoma and ovarian dysgerminoma are histologic twins.

blocks.text: Very high hCG produces systemic effects because hCG shares its alpha subunit with LH, FSH, and TSH and its beta subunit resembles that of LH. Acting like LH, hCG stimulates Leydig cells and testicular aromatase, raising estradiol and causing gynecomastia; at very high levels it weakly activates TSH receptors and can cause hyperthyroidism. A small primary with widespread lung metastases and a huge hCG is the classic choriocarcinoma picture.

blocks.predict: A 26-year-old man has a testicular mass called seminoma on biopsy, but his serum AFP is clearly elevated. What does the AFP tell you?
blocks.explain: Pure seminoma does not make AFP. An elevated AFP means yolk sac tumor elements are present, so this is a mixed or nonseminomatous germ cell tumor, which behaves more aggressively than pure seminoma.

sections.title: Leydig cell tumor and testicular lymphoma

blocks.text: Leydig cell tumor is the most common sex cord-stromal tumor of the testis. It occurs in boys and in men of any adult age. It forms a well-circumscribed, golden-brown nodule; the color comes from lipid and lipofuscin in the abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Reinke crystals, rod-shaped eosinophilic cytoplasmic crystalloids, are characteristic but present in only a minority of tumors. Most are benign; roughly 10% behave in a malignant way, usually in older men.

The clinical picture depends on the hormone and the patient's age. Leydig cells normally make testosterone, and testosterone can be aromatized to estradiol, so a Leydig cell tumor can produce androgen, estrogen, or both.

blocks.title: Hormonal effects of a Leydig cell tumor
rows: Precocious pseudopuberty: penile growth, pubic hair, deep voice, rapid growth
Autonomous testosterone; LH and FSH are suppressed, so it is GnRH-independent
Tumor estrogen (direct secretion and aromatization) stimulates breast tissue and suppresses gonadotropins and normal testosterone
blocks.caption: In an adult the extra testosterone is masked by normal levels, so estrogen effects are what is noticed.

blocks.text: Testicular lymphoma is the most common testicular tumor in men over 60. Germ cell tumors are rare at that age, so a testicular mass in an older man should suggest lymphoma first. Most cases are diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. The tumor infiltrates between seminiferous tubules and often replaces the testis diffusely. It is frequently bilateral at diagnosis or later, and it has a tendency to spread to the central nervous system and other extranodal sites such as skin and Waldeyer ring; one proposed explanation is that the testis and brain are both immune-privileged sites. Its prognosis is worse than that of germ cell tumors.

blocks.title: Testicular mass by age
rows: Germ cell tumors: nonseminomatous in the 20s, seminoma in the 30s
Lymphoma; spermatocytic tumor is a rare alternative
blocks.caption: Age is the first clue in any testicular mass question.

sections.title: Vaginal tumors: squamous cell carcinoma, clear cell adenocarcinoma, and sarcoma botryoides

blocks.text: Primary vaginal cancer is rare; most malignant tumors in the vagina are extensions or metastases from the cervix, endometrium, or vulva. The three primary tumors that boards test each occur in a distinct age group, and each age group is explained by a different cause.

blocks.title: Primary vaginal malignancies
rows: High-risk HPV; vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia (VAIN); prior cervical neoplasia
Bleeding or discharge; mass usually in upper posterior vagina
Young women, typically late teens to 20s
In utero diethylstilbestrol (DES) exposure; vaginal adenosis
Glandular tumor with clear, glycogen-rich cells and hobnail cells
Malignant tumor of primitive skeletal muscle cells
Soft, polypoid, grape-like mass protruding from the vagina; desmin and myogenin positive
blocks.caption: Age separates the three almost by itself.

blocks.text: Vaginal squamous cell carcinoma uses the same HPV mechanism as cervical cancer and arises from VAIN, which is graded like CIN. Women with previous cervical HSIL or carcinoma are at higher risk because the whole lower genital tract shares the infection. Lymphatic spread depends on level: the upper vagina drains to the iliac nodes like the cervix, and the lower vagina drains to the inguinal nodes like the vulva.

DES is a synthetic nonsteroidal estrogen that was given to pregnant women from the 1940s to 1971. In the exposed female fetus it disrupted the normal replacement of Mullerian glandular epithelium by squamous epithelium in the vagina, leaving persistent glands called vaginal adenosis. A small fraction of exposed daughters, roughly 1 in 1,000, developed clear cell adenocarcinoma in this tissue. DES daughters also have structural changes such as a T-shaped uterus and cervical ridges. The disease has become rare as this cohort has aged.

Sarcoma botryoides is a botryoid embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma. It grows beneath the vaginal mucosa, pushing it out into soft polypoid clusters that resemble grapes. Under the epithelium the tumor cells condense into a dense cambium layer. Because the cells are primitive skeletal muscle (rhabdomyoblasts, sometimes with cross-striations), they express the muscle markers desmin, myogenin, and MyoD1. It presents with vaginal bleeding or a mass protruding from the introitus in a very young girl.

sections.title: HPV-related and HPV-independent vulvar carcinoma

blocks.text: About 90% of vulvar cancers are squamous cell carcinomas. Like cervical and penile carcinoma, vulvar carcinoma follows two separate pathways. They differ in patient age, background skin, precursor, and genetics, and recognizing which pathway fits a case is the main exam skill.

blocks.title: Two pathways to vulvar squamous cell carcinoma
rows: Other HPV lesions of cervix, vagina, or anus; often multifocal
Lichen sclerosus or chronic lichen simplex
Usual (HPV-related) VIN, also called vulvar HSIL
HPV 16 E6 and E7; diffuse p16 staining
TP53 mutation; aberrant p53 staining; HPV negative
Well differentiated, keratinizing with keratin pearls
blocks.caption: The same split appears in penile and some head and neck squamous carcinomas.

blocks.text: The HPV-related pathway is the familiar one: high-risk HPV infects the vulvar squamous epithelium, E6 and E7 disable p53 and RB, and full-thickness dysplasia develops before invasion. Smoking and immunodeficiency promote persistence, which is why these patients are younger and often have lesions at other lower genital sites.

The HPV-independent pathway arises from chronically inflamed skin. Lichen sclerosus produces thin, white, parchment-like skin with epidermal atrophy and a band of dermal sclerosis, causing itching and scarring. Years of inflammation and repair select keratinocytes with TP53 mutations, which form differentiated VIN and then invasive carcinoma. Only a small percentage of women with lichen sclerosus develop carcinoma, but most HPV-independent carcinomas arise on such a background.

Vulvar carcinoma presents with itching, a persistent plaque, an ulcer, or a mass, sometimes with bleeding. Because itching from lichen sclerosus is common, a new nodule or nonhealing ulcer is the change that matters. Spread is to the superficial inguinal nodes, then the deep femoral nodes, then pelvic nodes; risk of nodal spread increases with depth of invasion. Midline tumors can drain to both groins.

sections.title: Vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia and extramammary Paget disease

blocks.text: Vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN) is the precursor of vulvar squamous carcinoma, and its two forms mirror the two carcinoma pathways. They look different under the microscope, which is why differentiated VIN is easy to miss.

blocks.title: Usual VIN and differentiated VIN
rows: Often multifocal white, red, or pigmented plaques
Usually a single thickened white or gray plaque on lichen sclerosus
Full-thickness atypia of basaloid cells, like CIN 3; koilocytes may be present
Atypia limited to the basal layers; upper cells look prematurely mature with abundant pink cytoplasm
Lower and slower progression; may regress
Higher and faster progression to carcinoma
blocks.caption: Differentiated VIN looks deceptively mature but carries the greater cancer risk.

blocks.text: Extramammary Paget disease of the vulva is an intraepithelial adenocarcinoma. Large pale tumor cells with abundant cytoplasm containing mucin spread through the epidermis singly and in clusters. They are thought to arise from glandular or apocrine-type progenitor cells within the epidermis and adnexa. The lesion is a red, moist, crusted, eczema-like plaque, often with a map-like border, that itches and is frequently treated for months as dermatitis. Because the cells spread within the epidermis well beyond the visible edge, recurrence is common.

blocks.title: Paget disease of the vulva and of the breast
rows: Usually arises within the epidermis or adnexa
Extension of an underlying ductal carcinoma into nipple skin
Usually absent; a minority have an adnexal carcinoma or an anorectal or urothelial primary
Nearly always present (ductal carcinoma in situ or invasive carcinoma)
Red, crusted, map-like plaque on vulva
Eczema-like scaling, crusting, or ulceration of the nipple and areola
blocks.caption: Similar cells, different meaning: in the breast, Paget cells signal a carcinoma beneath.

blocks.text: Paget cells must be distinguished from melanoma and from pagetoid spread of squamous neoplasia. Paget cells contain mucin (PAS-positive, diastase-resistant) and express CK7 and CEA, whereas melanoma cells lack mucin and express S100 and SOX10.

integration.text: Most tumors in this chapter can be predicted from a few mechanisms. High-risk HPV links microbiology to pathology across the cervix, vagina, vulva, penis, and anus: E6 removes p53, E7 removes RB, and persistence depends on cell-mediated immunity, which is why smoking and HIV matter. Where HPV is absent, chronic inflammation (lichen sclerosus, phimosis) and TP53 mutation take its place. In the endometrium, the balance of estrogen and progesterone, together with PTEN and mismatch repair genes, decides between orderly cycling, hyperplasia, and carcinoma, and the same endocrine logic explains why granulosa cell tumors cause hyperplasia and why fibroids shrink after menopause.

Anatomy and embryology predict spread and markers. The parametrial course of the ureters explains death from renal failure in cervical cancer; valveless vertebral veins explain prostate metastases to the lumbar spine; descent of the testis from the posterior abdominal wall explains para-aortic nodal spread; and the open peritoneal cavity explains why serous carcinoma presents late. Germ cell and sex cord-stromal tumors make the products of the tissues they copy, so AFP, hCG, LDH, estrogen, androgen, and thyroid hormone each point to a cell type. The limits are real: markers such as PSA and CA-125 are organ- or tissue-related, not cancer-specific, and a definite diagnosis always rests on histology.

summary: High-risk HPV causes CIN by E6 degradation of p53 and E7 inactivation of RB in the transformation zone; koilocytes mark infection, and grade depends on the thickness of atypical immature cells.
Most CIN 1 regresses; persistence of HPV 16 or 18, smoking, and immunodeficiency drive progression to HSIL and invasive carcinoma.
Cervical carcinoma presents with postcoital bleeding and kills through lateral parametrial spread that obstructs the ureters and causes postrenal failure.

Unopposed estrogen and PTEN loss lead to endometrial hyperplasia; atypical hyperplasia is the precursor of endometrioid carcinoma, whereas serous carcinoma arises in atrophic endometrium with TP53 mutation.
Leiomyomas are common, estrogen-sensitive, monoclonal, and benign; leiomyosarcomas arise de novo and are recognized by atypia, mitoses, and tumor cell necrosis.

Prostate carcinoma arises in the peripheral zone, is graded by gland pattern (Gleason), raises PSA, and spreads through the vertebral venous plexus to make osteoblastic metastases with high alkaline phosphatase.

Ovarian tumors are classified as surface epithelial, germ cell, or sex cord-stromal; high-grade serous carcinoma carries TP53 and often BRCA mutations, starts in the tubal fimbria, and spreads through the peritoneum with ascites and raised CA-125.

Germ cell and stromal tumors make what their cell of origin makes: AFP (yolk sac), hCG (choriocarcinoma), LDH (dysgerminoma), thyroid hormone (struma ovarii), estrogen (granulosa cell), and androgen (Sertoli-Leydig, Leydig).

Testicular germ cell tumors arise from GCNIS with isochromosome 12p, present as painless solid masses that do not transilluminate, and spread to para-aortic nodes; lymphoma is the most common testicular tumor after 60.

Lower genital tract squamous carcinomas follow an HPV-related pathway in younger patients and an HPV-independent, TP53-driven pathway on lichen sclerosus in older patients; vulvar Paget disease, unlike breast Paget disease, usually lacks an underlying carcinoma.

verify: Percentages vary between sources and should be checked against the reference NABNE uses: CIN 1 regression (about 60%), squamous versus adenocarcinoma share of cervical cancer (about 75 to 80% versus 15 to 20%), HPV 16 and 18 share of cervical cancer (about 70%), endometrioid versus serous share (about 80% versus 10 to 15%), and ovarian tumor group proportions.
The risk of carcinoma with atypical endometrial hyperplasia is given only as a large fraction because published figures range widely; hyperplasia without atypia is given as about 1 to 3%.
Lifetime ovarian cancer risk with BRCA1 (about 40%) and BRCA2 (about 10 to 20%) and the share of high-grade serous carcinomas with BRCA loss vary between series.

Leiomyosarcoma criteria (at least two of diffuse moderate to severe atypia, about 10 or more mitoses per 10 high-power fields, and coagulative tumor cell necrosis) follow the commonly used Stanford criteria; confirm the version expected.

Terminology has changed: WHO now uses LSIL and HSIL for CIN and VIN, atypical hyperplasia or endometrioid intraepithelial neoplasia for endometrium, germ cell neoplasia in situ for intratubular germ cell neoplasia, and spermatocytic tumor for spermatocytic seminoma. Confirm whether NABNE items use the older or newer names, and whether the molecular classes of endometrial carcinoma (POLE, mismatch repair deficient, p53 abnormal, no specific profile) are expected.
The route by which Krukenberg tumors reach the ovary and the mechanism of fluid formation in Meigs syndrome are not settled; the chapter states the leading explanations only.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: cin-grading (epithelial thickness replaced in CIN 1, 2, and 3), cervix-ureter-anatomy (parametrium with ureter beneath the uterine artery), and ovarian-tumor-tree (three origin groups with their members and markers).
